coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies

ILO launched a voluntary Standard Employment Contract for live-in and live-out domestic workers on 11 Sep 2025. Proposed Employment Act not confirmed enacted. No mandatory recurring duty found.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: One search returned no Sri Lankan sources. No national scrap-metal licensing regime found. Unverified whether local-authority or CEA licences apply.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: Pawnbrokers Ordinance No. 13 of 1942 (licence from Divisional Secretary, security deposit). Provincial statutes now set fees and deposits: Western Province registration Rs 50,000 plus annual Rs 25,000; North Western gazette (March 2025) requires a Rs 200,000 security deposit. Fragmented by province. The gazette fetch returned 503, so details are from search snippets. No second-hand dealer regime found.

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: NGJA requires jewellers to issue a certificate to customers (carat/PPT, trademark, price) under the Assaying and Hallmarking Regulations; licence cancellation for non-compliance (Sunday Times, Dec 2023, per search snippet). No mandatory-hallmark gazette for 2025 found. Related to K05 but a different buyer group (retail jewellers).

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: No Sri Lankan dismantler or end-of-life vehicle regime found. DMT removes vehicles with no revenue licence for 5 years from its system (May 2023). Nothing mandatory for parts dealers.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: Animals Act 1958: transport permit from District/Divisional Secretary, valid 2 weeks, needs a government vet health certificate, ear tags Rs 20/animal, Rs 50/animal fee. DAPH guidelines are from a 2009 gazette. African swine fever movement relaxation from 4 Nov 2024; current status unknown.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: Butchers Ordinance: annual or temporary licence from the local authority. Private slaughterhouses also need an Environmental Protection Licence and Factories Ordinance registration. Licences are issued per local authority, so fragmented. No central register.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No search spent (budget used on categories with clearer regulators). Unverified.

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: Veterinary Surgeons and Practitioners Act No. 46 of 1956: individual registration with the Veterinary Council. No premises licensing or medicine-seller register found. Low volume of buyers.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Water Resources Board: 2017 report says tube well builders must register; 2017 gazette requires WRB supervision of groundwater use for certain projects. Proposed annual well permit (Rs 7,500-15,000) under WRB Act amendments, enactment unconfirmed. No official WRB page found.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: CEA scheduled waste licence (Regulations No. 1 of 2008, Schedule VIII) covers collect/transport/store/recycle. No result on septage haulers. Unverified.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: Factories Ordinance: 2019 regulations (boiler registration, examination certificates, accredited inspectors reporting to the Chief Factory Inspecting Engineer) presented to Parliament; final gazette status unconfirmed. Lift examination under the 1960 regulations. Owners are mainly factories.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: Community-based organisations (3,400+ rural schemes) are registered with the Department of National Community Water Supply. CBOs have no clear legal mandate and often lack treatment and quality control. No tariff or regulator duty found.

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: Control of Pesticides Act 1980: Registrar licenses importers, formulators and sellers. Agro-dealers must hold NVQ Level 4 (provisional licence, full certification after 4 years' experience; per 2025 PlantwisePlus blog). Fertiliser dealer rules not found.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: SLBFE licensed foreign employment agencies: annual renewal (apply 30 days before expiry), Rs 5m bank guarantee, minimum 60 recruits/year, internal reports (conciliation, investigation, legal, trafficking, finance/cess), ABCD reports, remittance updates, branch records, inspections. Fee revised July 2023.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: No search spent (budget). Unverified.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: NGO Secretariat Dec 2024 directive requires all NGOs to register with it; Supreme Court petition filed Jan 2025 (outcome not found). Draft NGO (Registration and Supervision) Bill 2026 would replace the 1980 VSSO Act, with portal registration, annual action plans and quarterly progress reports, still in consultation (Oct 2026). Halal certification is voluntary, run by private certifiers (ACJU, HAC); no mandatory register.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: NTC issues private bus route permits (tender); 2026 gazette sets permit transfer rules (written or electronic application, 25% cap per route). School service permits under a 2013 gazette; 2023 gazette fee schedule (annual registration Rs 10,000 bus, Rs 3,000 van, unverified applicability). K13 already covers three-wheelers. No digital ticketing mandate found.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: Money changers: Central Bank permits under Foreign Exchange Act No. 12 of 2017; only 59 permits in 2025 plus 6 finance companies and 12 hotels, so a tiny buyer pool. Street vendors and market traders not searched.

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: Driving schools: about 1,500 schools, 800 registered, 700 not; registration restarted July 2024; Motor Traffic Regulations No. 1 of 2015 (A/B/C categories, licensed instructors, 2021 amendment, 40-novice monthly cap reported). Day care: provincial statutes (Southern 2019, Uva 2014) plus 2019 national guidelines, no uniform register. Food: labelling and trans-fat regulations in force from 1 July 2026. Tattoo studios and hunting outfitters not applicable or not found.

candidates.evidence: Act text: https://documents.gov.lk/view/acts/2026/3/09-2026_E.pdf. Summary: https://www.ft.lk/columns/A-new-era-for-microfinance-and-money-lending-in-Sri-Lanka/4-785554. News: https://www.dailymirror.lk/breaking-news/New-microfinance-authority-law-comes-into-force-replacing-2016-Act/108-335939. Sources conflict on commencement: the Daily Mirror says in force immediately, but the Act text says by Minister's Gazette order.

candidates.name: Moneylender and microfinance licence-readiness and records tool (MCRA Act No. 9 of 2026)
candidates.trigger: The Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Authority Act No. 9 of 2026 (passed 4 Mar 2026) replaces the 2016 Microfinance Act. All moneylenders need an annual licence displayed at each location. Existing moneylenders get 24 months to apply; MFIs under the old Act have 12 months to comply. Prior approval is needed for new branches, outsourced debt collection and capital reductions (penalties up to Rs 2m). The Authority inspects records and keeps sector databases.
candidates.unchecked: Whether the commencement order has been gazetted. Exact periodic return and register formats. Whether pawnbrokers are covered. The prescribed application timeframe. Competitor search NOT run (budget exhausted): the required form was sinhala/English '<software> + money lending licence + microfinance Sri Lanka'.

The regulator is weak (PHSRC secretary says it lacks staff and its gazettes have been pending about 10 years). No insurer or state-scheme billing duty found. Weak candidate only.

coverage.category: 25. Pharmacies, medicine importers, and users of controlled chemicals or precursors
coverage.found: The NMRA pharmacy renewal is K09 (rejected). The Precursor Control Authority at NDDCB (Act No. 1 of 2008) requires licences, premises registration and per-import notification, and issued 2026 notices on mixtures and special-surveillance chemicals. The buyer group is a small number of chemical importers. Weak candidate only.

coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: SLBFE-licensed foreign employment agencies renew annually with a bank guarantee and a performance review, filed on paper forms. Digitisation was approved by Cabinet in Mar 2024, and a new SLBFE Act to replace Act No. 21 of 1985 was expected in 2026 (not confirmed passed). Local security and cleaning agencies: nothing found.

coverage.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
coverage.found: CIDA contractor registration lasts 3 years; online renewal exists for grades C3 and above. Low frequency, and the portal partly covers it. Mining and quarry (GSMB licences) not searched. Weak candidate only.

coverage.category: 28. Notaries, land agents, real estate brokers and other professionals with periodic or anti-money-laundering reports
coverage.found: Under the FTRA No. 6 of 2006, the FIU's DNFBP rules (Gazette 2053/20 of 2018) cover real estate agents, lawyers, notaries, accountants, gem dealers and trust or company service providers. The FIU fined 4 non-financial businesses between Oct 2025 and Mar 2026. Gem dealers are covered by K05. No sector-specific software gap confirmed.

coverage.category: 29. Hotels, guest houses and short-term rentals: guest registers, tourism levies
coverage.found: SLTDA registration is mandatory and renewed annually under Act No. 38 of 2005. The eServices portal exists. The Tourism Development Levy is paid only by bank transfer with a slip uploaded to the system. 2026 renewal and TDL filing details were not found. Homestays are K06.

coverage.category: 30. Small exporters and importers facing traceability or certification rules: food, fish, timber, forest-risk commodities
coverage.found: Ceylon Cinnamon is an EU PGI. Exporters must belong to the CCGIA, run a three-level control plan, and be licensed by the EDB. UNIDO already built a blockchain traceability platform. Fishing vessels: the VMS mandate is expanding in 2026. Rubber EUDR is K02, timber is K04, CATCH is K10.

coverage.category: 31. Environmental Protection Licence (CEA / local authorities)
coverage.found: Annual EPL renewal for categories A-D (Gazette 2264/18 of Jan 2022: 33+71+56+39 activities). CEA closed 41 factories in 2025 for not renewing. A July 2026 fatal factory fire led to promised inspections. See candidate.

coverage.category: 32. Moneylenders and microfinance (Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Authority Act No. 9 of 2026)
coverage.found: New licensing of moneylenders and microfinance institutions (MFIs). About 11,000 MFIs were estimated in Nov 2023 versus 4 registered. See candidate.

coverage.category: 33. Excise liquor licences (wine stores, bars, hotel and restaurant licences)
coverage.found: About 4,500 retail liquor licences renewed annually (Jan 2025 Daily Mirror). Tax clearance is customarily requested. The Oct 2025 gazette set tax-arrears suspension rules for production licences. No online renewal portal confirmed.

coverage.category: 34. Vehicle emission testing (DMT)
coverage.found: The emission test is tied to the annual revenue licence. LAUGFS Eco Sri alone runs 87 fixed centres and 27 mobile units, and its officers' entries are linked to the DMT system. Not a viable gap.

coverage.category: 35. Fisheries: multi-day vessel registration, VMS and logbooks (DFAR)
coverage.found: The High Seas Regulations as amended in 2022 bar registration, renewal and departure approval for multi-day vessels without VMS. Of 5,200 multi-day vessels, 4,200 have VMS. In July 2026 Cabinet approved VMS for about 1,500 more vessels at government cost. Logbooks have been required since 2012 and are cross-checked against VMS tracks.

coverage.category: 36. Weights and measures verification (Measurement Units, Standards and Services Dept)
coverage.found: Act No. 35 of 1995 requires periodic examination and stamping of weighing and measuring instruments. A verification certificate must be kept with each instrument. The verification interval was not confirmed.

coverage.category: 37. Pre-schools and early childhood centres
coverage.found: No national Act. Registration is provincial (e.g. Central Province charter, Gazette 1999/32 of 2016). The ministry said in June 2026 that unregistered pre-schools are a major challenge. Tuition classes: nothing found.

coverage.category: 38. Rice mills and Paddy Marketing Board registration
coverage.found: Millers registered with the PMB are invited by Cabinet and Sathosa to mill and supply rice (2025-2026 decisions). No filing duty found beyond registration.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No mandatory beekeeper registration, licence or reporting duty found in 3 searches (EN and Sinhala) or in the Daily Mirror article of 26 May 2026. About 17,000 beekeepers, about 50 t honey a year against about 200 t demand, imports from India, Australia and China. The Dept of Agriculture offers 50% subsidies on bee boxes and kits, and training at the Bee Development Unit in Badulla. Only export-market approvals found (Saudi SFDA list, 2020). No duty means no recurring-report software hook. Not checked: SLSI honey standard, the Export Development Board and Dept of Animal Production and Health roles, and whether the subsidy needs a registration.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: Funeral endowment societies (maranadhara samithi, about 25,000 per a single 2022 blog on minormatters.org, unverified) must register with the Divisional Secretariat and file accounts and reports there. Legal basis, form and frequency not confirmed. No software found for them in English or Sinhala searches. Cemeteries are run by councils under Ordinance 9 of 1899 and Ordinance 57 of 1946, and council crematoria need a cremation licence (2018 gazette rules). Colombo abolished burial and cremation fees for residents. No licensing regime for private funeral parlours found. A 2025 COPA hearing exposed an unauthorised parlour at Borella cemetery. Mosque and incorporated janaza societies exist (e.g. Maligawatta Janaza Society Act 5 of 2010, audited accounts). Not checked: the legal basis and reporting forms for funeral societies, parlour licensing in individual councils, and the Social Services Act.

result.competitor: No commercial agency-side compliance or renewal product found. The only agency systems I found were University of Colombo (UCSC) thesis projects built for single agencies (Foreign Recruitment Handling System 2016, Online Foreign Employment Agency Management System 2018, Jobshop 2013). SLBFE runs its own portals: services.slbfe.lk login, the applications.slbfe.lk valid-agency list, and a web system where foreign employers enter job orders. In March 2024 the Cabinet approved digitising the whole foreign employment sector; I could not confirm whether it has gone live or whether it covers agency renewal and reporting. That plan could later absorb the core job. I did not run a Sinhala-language search.
result.duty: SLBFE Act No. 21 of 1985 licensing. Agency licences last one year and are renewable; the renewal application is due 30 days before expiry. Requirements per slbfe.lk ?p=1011: at least 60 recruits a year; conciliation, investigation, legal, trafficking and finance (cess) reports, which appear to be SLBFE's internal reports on the agency; ABCD reports from the agency; up-to-date remittances and cess; business registration, lease or deed, and floor plan; a Rs 5m bank guarantee; office inspection, interview and agreement. Fee: Rs 100,000 plus SSCL and VAT (a July 2023 gazette set it at Rs 117,949 tax-inclusive). Branch renewal is 75% of the fee. Penalty: without renewal the agency cannot operate. Enforcement is active: 1,003 agencies were suspended in 2024 and 805 had legal action started against them in 2025 (The Morning, Mar 2026). Not verified: the format of the ABCD reports, and whether renewal can be submitted online. The page was last updated Jan 2024. I found no enacted amendment Act.
result.market: I could not confirm the number of licensed agencies; the SLBFE pages show no total. Indirect signals: 1,163 suspensions in 2020-2025, including 1,003 in 2024, and about 311,000 placements in 2024 with a target of 340,000 for 2025. My rough estimate is several hundred to about 1,500 licensees. This is unverified.
result.reason: The duty is real. The SLBFE says an agency licence lasts one year and must be renewed, with the application due 30 days before expiry. Renewal requires at least 60 recruits a year, cleared remittances and cess, ABCD reports, a Rs 5m bank guarantee, an office inspection and an interview. The fee is Rs 100,000 plus taxes. I found no agency-side compliance software, only university thesis systems built for single agencies. However, the conciliation, investigation, legal, trafficking and cess reports appear to be the SLBFE's own internal reports on the agency, so the agency's part is mostly a document pack once a year. The buyer pool is small: probably under about 1,500 agencies, though I could not confirm a count. Renewal comes once a year, and much of the review depends on SLBFE data, so there is little for a product to do. Buyers are reachable through agency associations, but willingness to pay is doubtful.

result.competitor: I found no compliance or licence-readiness product. General loan-management software sold in Sri Lanka does exist: LoanMaster by POS Masters (pawning centres and microfinance, replaces paper ledgers), Kredible (cloud microfinance system built in Sri Lanka), CloudBankin (used by Sejaya Micro Credit), plus custom builds on Fiverr. If the Authority prescribes formats, any of these could add regulatory reports. There is no state portal yet.
result.duty: Act No. 9 of 2026 (Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Authority Act) was certified and gazetted on 20 Mar 2026. Under s.1(2), every provision except the citation section comes into force only on a date the Minister appoints by Gazette Order. Searches in English and Sinhala found no commencement order. The Daily Mirror (21 Mar 2026) says it came into force immediately, which conflicts with the Act text. According to the FT.lk summary: all moneylenders need a licence valid for one year; microfinance licences last three years; existing moneylenders may operate for 24 months but must apply within a prescribed timeframe; MFIs licensed under the 2016 Act must comply within 12 months; prior approval is needed for key changes; penalties go up to Rs 2m; the Authority can inspect records. Not verified: record and return formats, whether pawnbrokers are covered (FT says MFIs may do pawning only with approval), and the application timeframe. I could not read the Act PDF itself (HTTP 404).
result.market: Not verified. The claim's figure of about 11,000 MFIs (Nov 2023) did not appear in this session's searches. FT.lk confirms only 4 institutions ever registered under the 2016 Act. The Daily Mirror (Feb 2026) says the Act treats microcredit providers registered as voluntary organisations or societies as moneylenders, which widens the pool, but gives no count. An industry body, the Lanka Microfinance Network, elected its first board on 15 May 2026 and could be a distribution channel.
result.reason: The Act is real. Act No. 9 of 2026 was certified on 20 Mar 2026 and repeals the 2016 Act. But s.1(2) says its operative provisions start only on a date the Minister sets by Gazette Order. I found no such order, no Authority board, no licensing window and no prescribed forms or returns. The Daily Mirror's report that it took effect "with immediate effect" contradicts the Act's own text. Nothing local does licence-readiness. Loan-ledger tools already exist: LoanMaster (pawning and microfinance), Kredible and CloudBankin. Buyers are informal lenders and NGO societies that resist being regulated and are hard to reach, and the critics say they cannot pay for audits. There is too little to build against until the regulations come out. Check again once the commencement order is gazetted.

result.competitor: No EPL software or tracker found. There is no online EPL application or renewal portal: CEA forms are downloaded and filed at regional or local offices. However, CEA joined GovPay on 26 Sept 2025, so licence, inspection and processing fees can be paid online. NWP PEA reports that renewal applications can be collected online. CEA-registered laboratories, consultants and specialists already support EPL applicants (emission measurements), and they likely handle the paperwork. I did not search for private consultancy firms by name. There is a risk that the state digitises the process after the 2026 regulatory reforms.
result.duty: Prescribed industries need an Environmental Protection Licence under the National Environmental Act (Gazette 2264/18 of 27.01.2022): 33 activities in Part A, 71 in B, 56 in C and 39 in D. Licences are valid for up to 1 year (A, B, non-mining), up to 2 years (C) and up to 3 years (D). Renewal must be filed 3 months before expiry using a one-page form, with an inspection fee. Fees are Rs 15,000 (A), 10,000 (B), 4,000 (C) and 4,500 (D). CEA regional offices or the BOI issue A-C licences. MC/UC/Pradeshiya Sabhas issue D licences (since 27.02.2022), with a technical committee for each local authority. North Western Province has its own PEA, which uses a 1-month renewal lead time. Enforcement: CEA permanently closed 41 factories in 2025 for non-renewal and temporarily closed 19 more. In July 2026, after the Homagama/Katuwana fire (the factory's EPL had not been renewed since 2024), the Deputy Minister said CEA lacks the power to shut factories, that amending regulations are coming, and that inspections would follow. Statutory fine amounts were not verified.
result.market: Not found. CEA annual reports (on parliament.lk) were not opened, and I found no total count of licence holders. Partial data: only 35 of 648 private laboratories hold an EPL (2024 audit), and only 7 of 12 BOI zones hold valid EPLs. 199 prescribed activity types. The number of licence holders is probably in the thousands to low tens of thousands, but this is unverified.
result.reason: The duty is real. Under the National Environmental Act, Gazette 2264/18 (2022) lists categories A-D (33/71/56/39 activities). Validity runs from 1 year (A, B) to 2-3 years (C, D). Renewal must be filed 3 months before expiry, with an inspection fee. CEA closed 41 factories in 2025 for non-renewal, and the July 2026 Homagama fire put pressure on the government. I found no EPL software. CEA forms are still on paper, but since Sept 2025 CEA fees can be paid on GovPay. The renewal form is one page, renewal is annual at most, and fees are Rs 4,000-15,000, so a tracker only reminds. Labs and consultants already do the paperwork for factories. North Western Province runs its own PEA. I found no count of licence holders. Willingness to pay is low.

Duty appears real (Animals Act 1958; DAPH guidelines; ASF gazette needing a vet health report, per Ada Derana). I could not read the DAPH guideline PDF (binary). Search found no digital permit system or software competitor for domestic movement. Cattle transport licences were suspended in 2017 (DGI, thecattlesite), and I did not confirm they resumed. Permits are issued by District Secretaries, so a vendor can't automate the issuing. Trader counts are unknown and the traders are informal, which makes them hard to reach and unlikely to pay. Enforcement is unclear, and the pain is a permit-getting step, not a recurring filing. Weak market.

Duty is real: Motor Traffic (Driving Schools, Instructors) Regulations No. 1 of 2015 require registration with the Commissioner General; the DMT restarted compulsory registration in mid-2024 (Daily Mirror, 1 July 2024). About 1,500 schools, 800 registered, 700 not. No deadline, penalty or recurring reporting duty was found. The 40-novice cap and new gazette were not verified, and there is no 2026 news. Local competitors exist: Imagini DriveMate, Digiscan and AutoDrive (sources are thin, mostly LinkedIn), so the core job is not unserved. Registration is one-off, which means low frequency. The market is small and has low willingness to pay. Weak fit.

DNCWS registers the CBOs that run community water schemes. Its 2024 report cites about 3,783 projects serving about 605k families, so the buyer count is real. I found no mandatory recurring test, report or billing duty on CBOs. The search did not reach the DNCWS rules or the Ministry of Health guidelines. I found no CBO-specific software, only utility-side NWSDB prototypes and India's NalJalSeva as a model. The buyers are volunteer rural committees with low willingness to pay, and DNCWS or donors would most likely build any tool. The duty is unconfirmed, so this stays unverifiable. Score is low because of the weak duty, the weak payer and a state-led channel.

The NGO Bill (Registration and Supervision), L.D.-O. 6/2026, is still a draft. The NGO Secretariat DG confirmed it is not enacted. Its June 2026 text is not public and is under restricted consultation. The reported terms are a Rs 1m fine, 3-year registration, and portal annual plans and quarterly reports. The existing duty is the Voluntary Social Services Act No. 31 of 1980, and the 2024 directive was not checked. I found no competing software, but I only searched news. I did not search for products. Buyers are unpaid volunteers with low willingness to pay. The duty is not yet in force, the rules are unsettled, and the state will run the portal, so an MVP cannot be specified. Not refuted, but weak.

The duty is real. The Control of Pesticides Act No. 33 of 1980 requires sellers to register with the Registrar of Pesticides. The 2011 gazette amendment requires an NVQ Level 4 "Agrochemical Sales and Technical Assistant" registration (or equivalent). That registration lasts 3 years and renewal needs a competency proof, a medical report and a fee. The 2025 PlantwisePlus blog confirms NVQ-4 with a provisional licence after 400 hours of training. I found no POS or compliance software for this job, but I also found no dealer count and no sales-register duty. The core obligation is a one-off training or certificate and a 3-yearly renewal, so frequency is low. The market is small and fragmented, buyers are low-tech, and the task is mostly paperwork, so willingness to pay is weak. I did not check whether enforcement is real.

The Factories Ordinance (Ch.128, ss.34-38A) covers steam boilers and pressure vessels. Parliament's August 2019 order paper lists regulations on boiler registration and on examination certificates. The press report says certified inspectors must report to the Chief Factory Inspecting Engineer. I could not read the boiler regulation text, so I could not confirm gazetting or enforcement, the renewal cycle, penalties or owner counts. The only gazette I found (2142/90, Sept 2019) is the factory registration regulations. I found no Sri Lankan boiler software or portal, but the search was thin. The market looks small and the buyers are fragmented. The workflow is largely a paper certificate and inspector relationship, and there is no public statistic on owners. Low score.
